glossary.title: The Stock Market Is Being Used as a Dumping Ground
glossary.llm_summary: This video discusses the structural shift in US technology IPO timing and valuation. It contrasts historical tech IPOs (Amazon at $430M, Google at $23B, Facebook at $100B) with modern mega-cap debuts (SpaceX at ~$1.8T, Anthropic and OpenAI targeting higher valuations). The speaker attributes this shift to three regulatory/structural changes: the 1996 National Securities Markets Improvement Act (raising the investor cap for private funds and allowing institutional capital into venture), the 2012 JOBS Act (raising the shareholder threshold from 500 to 2,000 and excluding employee stock options from the count), and tender offers enabling liquidity without IPOs. The thesis: companies now mature privately, capturing most growth value before listing; the public market is offered "asymmetric bets pointed the wrong way" — requiring SpaceX to reach 0.25x the US stock market for a 10x return. No analysis of commodities, rates, currencies, China, ASX, miners, or geopolitics.
glossary.transcript_text: You've probably seen this chart that's going viral right now. This bar is every tech company that's gone public in America through an initial public offering since 1980. That's 45 years of some of the most successful companies in history, the entire dot bubble, and thousands of other companies. Add up what every one of them was worth on their first day of trading and you get about $4.1 trillion. This other bar is just three companies, SpaceX, Anthropic, and Open AAI. SpaceX went public in June in the biggest initial public offering in history. Anthropic and Open AI are lining up to be next. When you add up what SpaceX was worth on its first day of trading and the prices Anthropic and Open AI are reportedly aiming for, you get about $5.2 trillion. That's three companies worth more than every tech IPO in America since 1980 combined. Which is why every conversation about these three companies ends up at the same question. Are they worth it? Wall Street analysts, famous investors, and everyone on Reddit have been arguing about it for months. But the better question is a lot simpler. It's how much value is even left. When Amazon went public in 1997, they were 3 years old and worth around $430 million. If you invested $1,000 into Amazon's initial public offering, it would be worth more than $3 million today. Which means almost all of Amazon's growth happened after the company went public. And the average Joe's like me and you were able to buy in. Now look at SpaceX. They sold shares at a price that valued the company at just under $1.8 trillion. For those buyers to get the same return Amazon's got, SpaceX would have to grow to become a $5.9 quadrillion company. That's more than 11 times all the personal wealth on Earth and the first time I've ever had to say the word quadrillion out loud. The difference is where they started. Amazon went public when they were worth around $430 million. SpaceX went public when they were worth more than 4,000 times that. Their growth story has already happened and the public markets just weren't invited to the party. That's the change hiding inside this chart. Companies used to go public to pay for their growth. Now they go public after they've grown. But this was also never just about any single IPO or even all three of them. A finance professor at Arizona State named Hendrickk Besson Bbinder went through a hundred years of the American stock market. He found that the typical stock actually lost money, which explains a lot about my brokerage account. But it also raises the question, where does all the money in the market come from? Well, over those hundred years, half of all the $91 trillion in net wealth the American stock market created came from just 46 companies. The top five companies alone made up about a fifth of it. And they all had one thing in common. They were all listed on the public markets early in their life. And when you add up what all five were worth when they went public, even after adjusting for inflation, it's less than the $75 billion SpaceX raised in just their public offering alone. Those same five companies are now worth about $21 trillion today. Which means almost all of that growth happened in public where anyone with a brokerage account could have participated in owning a piece of it. That's the part that's changing. Last year, Andre Horowitz, one of the most successful venture capital firms in history, published a blog post called Private Markets Are the New High Growth Public Markets. They found that the typical company that went public between 2014 and 2019 generated about 80% of its value after it listed. But the typical company from 2020 to 2023 created more than half of its value before it was ever listed, which is a venture capital firm basically telling you that the best part now happens on their side of the fence. This summer, Vanguard, one of the world's biggest investment companies, put out a report titled private longer, public later, which isn't the most comforting headline from a company built on the public stock market. In this report, Vanguard added up every private startup in the world worth at least a billion. In 2016, together they were worth about $800 billion. By this spring, that number was about 8.6 trillion. That's trillions of dollars of growth that never traded on a stock exchange and never gave the public a chance to invest in. For most of the last century, three things pushed a young, fast-growing company into the public markets. Over the last 30 years, all three of those stopped working. And that changed something much bigger. It changed where the money actually goes. But before I get into that, let's take a minute to talk about something else that quietly influences where the money goes in our society. Most loyalty programs are designed to change your behavior. They want you to fly this airline or shop at that store. And they do it because it works. According to Bond's 2026 loyalty report, 73% of loyalty members said a program gets them to spend more. Which brings us to the sponsor of today's video, Built. They take a different approach. Built is the loyalty program for where you live and it rewards you with points on every housing payment at any home. Which means a payment you were already making finally starts earning you points. And it doesn't stop at home. Link your credit cards and you can earn built points on your everyday spending at more than 50,000 partner businesses. You can redeem your built points toward stays and flights with Hyatt, Marriott, United, and Alaska or toward lift rides, Amazon purchases, fitness classes, and more. Personally, I'd redeem mine toward an Apple gift card. So, if you're not already earning points on your rent and mortgage payments, you need to check out Built. Over 7 million members already use Built, and there's no cost to join. If you're interested, you can start earning points on your rent and mortgage payments when you sign up through the link in my description or by using the QR code on screen. And make sure to use my URL so they know I sent you. Thank you to Built for sponsoring this video. Now, back to how the stock market went from a company's first stop to its last. Throughout history, if you were a fast growing company that needed real money, there was really only one place to find it. That was the stock market. Going public wasn't a victory lap. It was where you went when you needed serious amounts of cash. When Amazon filed to go public in 1997, they said exactly this. They said, "The company has no specific plan for the net proceeds of this offering. The company expects to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, including working capital to fund anticipated operating losses and capital expenditures, which is them pretty much saying, "We're going to be spending a lot of money, and our company doesn't generate enough on its own." But the year before Amazon went public was also where things were beginning to change. Congress passed a new law called the National Securities Markets Improvement Act. Before 1996, a private investment fund like the venture capital funds that back startups could only have a 100 investors. Which means if you wanted to raise a billion dollar private investment fund, every one of those hundred investors had to bring an average of $10 million. So during this time, private funds relied on a small number of ultra-wealthy individuals to write massive checks, which is why most private funds were smaller and why there just wasn't enough capital in the private markets to go around. But this new law removed the 100 person cap as long as every investor in the fund was what's called a qualified purchaser, which is an individual with at least $5 million in investments or an institution with at least $25 million. This opened the door for institutional capital to flood into private markets. It meant pension funds, university endowments, and other investors with deep pockets could now pour money into venture capital. And over time, hedge funds and even mutual funds started buying into startups, which meant the biggest pools of money in the world were now entering the private markets. Two economist, Michael Euans and Joan Fairmensa, measured what happened next. The $1.3 billion going into latestage startups in 1995 grew to 11.4 billion by 2005 and then to $33 billion by 2015. That same year, companies going public through an initial public offering raised about $22 billion. So by 2015, latestage startups were raising more money privately than every company going public through an initial public offering, which means a company didn't need the stock market to access capital anymore. They could get the same capital they needed from private investment funds without ever having to deal with the public. But it wasn't just this one rule change that caused this shift. The money was only the first thing to stop working. The second was a rule that used to drag companies onto the stock market, whether they wanted to go or not. In 1964, Congress implemented a rule to securities law called section 12G, which sounds like a seat you get on a budget airline. The rule said that once a company of any real size had 500 shareholders, it had to start reporting like a public company. This acted as a trigger that pushed private companies into a public reporting regime. The same way a public company reports its financials, a private company would have to file quarterly reports, an annual report, and an update every time something big happened, which was a huge deal for startups because startups pay people in stock. Every employee who got shares instead of a bigger paycheck was one more shareholder on the way to 500. This was the law that forced some of the most successful companies in American history to go public when they did. It started with Microsoft in the 80s. To attract managers and programmers, Microsoft had been selling them shares and handing out stock options. By 1987, Microsoft estimated more than 500 people would own its stock, which would force the company to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission. John Shirley, the former president and chief operating officer, said a projection of stock ownership showed we'd have to make a public offering at some point. So, Microsoft decided not to wait around, and in 1986, they went public. But it wasn't just Microsoft that hit this wall. When Google filed to go public in 2004, the founders explained it about as directly as you can. By law, certain private companies must report as if they were public companies. The deadline imposed by this requirement accelerated our decision. Then there was also Facebook. Mark Zuckerberg was never in a hurry to go public. Back in 2010, Zuck flat out said it, "We aren't planning to go public anytime soon." Then he continued by saying, "I tend to think that being private is better for us right now because of some of the big risk we want to take in developing new products." And Facebook didn't need the money. They were the hottest startup in the world and everyone wanted in, which is how in January 2011, Facebook announced it had just raised $1.5 billion privately. But in that same announcement, Facebook said it expected to pass 500 shareholders sometime that year, which meant they would have to start publishing their financials no later than April 30th, 2012. So Facebook was about to get the worst of both worlds. They were about to have to put their numbers out in the open for every competitor to be able to read without any of the upside of actually being a public company like a large infusion of equity capital and having liquidity for its stock. So, in 2012, Facebook took its stock public. And on May 18th, before Facebook's first day of trading, Zuckerberg gave a short speech right before ringing NASDAQ's opening bell. He said, "Going public is an important milestone in our history. But here's the thing. Our mission isn't to be a public company." Which is a funny thing to say on the day you become one, but to be fair, it's also probably one of the least weird things Zuck has said. >> You drink coffee, man, or no? >> Nah. >> Really? Yeah. >> I mean, you've you've had it. >> I have. Um, sometimes on vacation, I'll drink it recreationally. It's like every once in a while. >> For almost 50 years, the 500 shareholder rule was quietly working in the public's favor. It dragged companies onto the stock market while they still had most of their growing left. But then on April 5th, 2012, it got rewritten. That's the day the Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act or the Jobs Act became law. And you just know somebody in Congress felt like a genius when they finally got the letters to spell jobs. It was supposed to help young growth companies access the public markets. The first part of the law is even titled Reopening American Capital Markets to emerging growth companies, but it also quietly rewrote the same law that forced some of the most successful companies in American history to go public when they did. The law that pushed Microsoft onto the stock market at about half a billion dollars, Google at 23 billion, and Facebook at a hundred billion was being rewritten. The Jobs Act raised the limit from 500 shareholders to 2,000 before triggering public disclosure requirements, and employees who received stock as compensation were excluded from the count entirely, which means most of the employees who pushed Microsoft toward 500 wouldn't even count today. So by 2012, startups had access to more private capital than ever. and the rule that used to drag them onto the stock market had now been changed, which left just one reason to go public still standing, the payday. It was the moment the people who built a company, the employees and early investors could finally turn their shares into actual money. Because a startup can be worth billions on paper, and its employees still have no easy way to sell their shares. Before 2012, a company could let its employees sell some of their shares privately, but every new investor who bought them was one more shareholder on the way to 500. But after the Jobs Act, that limit was now four times higher. Companies could now run these sales over and over without ever worrying about hitting the cap. They did this through what's called a tender offer. It's kind of like a yard sale a company runs for its own stock. Employees and early investors bring their shares. Invited investors show up with cash, and nobody ever goes near a public stock exchange. Stripe is one of the best examples. If you've bought anything online, there's a decent chance Stripe handled the payment. Stripe was founded in 2010. 16 years later, it's one of the most valuable companies on Earth, and it still isn't public. Instead, Stripe keeps running these tender offers. In February 2024, Stripe's tender offer valued the company at $65 billion. The latest one, just a few months ago, valued Stripe at $159 billion. That's almost hundred billion of growth in 2 years that you and I weren't able to buy a single share of. Stripe's co-founder, John Collison, was asked on Bloomberg whether Stripe would ever go public. He said, "Presumably at some stage," which is the business version of running into someone at a bar and saying, "We should totally hang out sometime." So, the 1996 law let big institutions pour money into private companies and startups stop needing the stock market's money. The Jobs Act rewrote the rule that used to push companies to go public. And tender offers let employees and early investors cash out without ever needing to go through an initial public offering. Put all three of these together and you get a new system. One where a company can grow into one of the most valuable companies on Earth without ever going public. And that's what's happening right now. 20 years ago, the typical company going public was just 5 years old. Last year, they were 14. Those extra 9 years are some of the best years of growth a company will ever have. And they used to happen on the stock market where anyone could buy in and fewer companies are making the trip at all. In 1996, 266 companies backed by venture capital went public. Last year, with more than 10 times as much venture money going into startups, only 49 did. So, if companies don't need the public markets anymore, why did SpaceX go public at all? And why are anthropic and OpenAI lining up next in line? Before I get to that, making this video meant reading a securities law from 1964, Amazon's regulatory filings, and a Facebook press release from 2011. I tried to do all the research so you wouldn't have to. If that's worth something to you, please hit subscribe. It helps the channel more than you'd think, and it keeps me making these videos. Now, back to the question of why companies are even going public at all. And it's because the reason companies go public has changed. A company now goes public after the private market has already created and captured most of its value. In March of last year, private investors valued Anthropic at $61.5 billion. This May, Anthropic was valued at $965 billion, more than 15 times higher in just over a year. And Anthropic's IPO is now reportedly aiming for about double that, which changes the shape of the bet the public gets offered. When Amazon went public, it was worth $430 million. It was a risky high growth bet, but one with almost unlimited room to grow. That's how a $1,000 investment can turn into 3 million. For growth companies going public back then, the worst case was the company went under. You lost your $1,000 and you had to suck it up and move on. But the best case was you never had to work again. You had a chance to invest in a company building the future before it was priced like it had already built the future. Investors call that an asymmetric bet. Risk a little for a shot at a lot. And that's where returns like Amazon's come from. But today, that's flipped. When a company goes public at nearly $2 trillion, you have to ask how much upside is even left. For SpaceX to deliver even a 10 times return from its offer price, it would have to be worth about a quarter of the entire American stock market. And for a 100 times, in order to get the same life-changing type of returns we saw with Amazon, SpaceX would have to be worth more than every public company on Earth combined. This isn't me saying these companies can't keep growing. It's me saying the public is being offered a very different bet than it used to get. People can keep arguing about whether these three companies deserve their valuations, but the reality is it doesn't matter what anyone thinks these companies are worth. Nobody buying at these prices is getting a good deal. They're still getting an asymmetric bet. Just this time it's pointed the wrong way. [music]

glossary.title: Trump Admits Unthinkable Dollar Reset
glossary.llm_summary: Felix Prehn, economist and former investment banker, analyzes a recent Time magazine interview in which Trump stated inflation will 'very rapidly' pay off US national debt and hinted at unspecified 'other means'. Prehn argues this confirms financial repression strategy: the government deliberately keeps Treasury yields below inflation to erode real debt burden. He cites a 2011 BIS study showing post-WWII financial repression erased 2–3% of economy debt annually in the US and UK. Current problem: 10-year Treasury yields exceed CPI, making debt more expensive. Required solution: force Fed rates to 1% or less, which Trump has publicly demanded and for which he has appointed a supportive Fed board member, with a rate meeting scheduled before year-end. Consequence: K-shaped wealth gap widens—asset holders (stocks, gold, property) gain as dollar debases; wage earners lose purchasing power. Gold now costs 137 labor-hours vs 20 in 2000 for US workers. Dollar reserve status erodes deliberately; central banks trimming reserves. Risk: 1,700 'zombie' corporate stocks burning cash in North America, unable to service debt. Prehn argues the plan is to debase the dollar just enough to lighten debt while managing capital-flight risks.

glossary.title: Deal Fever: NST Dodges, LYC Deals
glossary.llm_summary:
Goldfields (South Africa) submitted non-binding proposal for Northern Star (ASX) on 13–14 September at 0.3125 GFI shares plus A$725 cash per share, implying A$38.7B equity value (A$27/share). NST board rejected further engagement on 24–25 September. Deal leaked to Bloomberg 26 September; speakers interpret as pressure tactic to mobilize NST shareholders (activist Elliot Management holds large stake). Goldfields CEO Mike Fraser claims A$4–5B USD synergies, ~50% from tax depreciation reset upon asset revaluation. GFI stock fell 13% after announcement; offer comprises 73% GFI script (ASX CDI with historical liquidity concerns). NST's interim leadership (CEO departed, replacement not appointed, chair exiting) questioned ability to resist activist pressure for deal completion.

Linus Resources agreed A$968M all-share acquisition of Meteoric Resources, implying ~6% dilution and 80% reserve addition via Calera ionic clay rare earth project (Brazil, claimed largest outside China). Linus stock fell 7%; Meteoric rose 44%. Reuters reported Linus halted CEO recruitment for 4.5 months during undisclosed change-of-control discussions with unnamed party (speculation: MP Materials, following failed 2024 merger talks); acquisition appears "plan B" strategic response. Integration questions persist regarding ionic clay processing through existing flowsheet at Malaysia facility.

Speakers identify tax depreciation reset synergies as abundant M&A driver in Australian mining, likely accelerating mid-tier consolidation. Broader observation: South African miners (Goldfields, Harmony) actively expanding in Australia while North American majors continue multi-year exit.

glossary.title: The Private Credit Shock is Worsening | Are we F**K'd
glossary.llm_summary: Meet Kevin reviews US credit market stress, arguing fears are overblown versus 2025 levels. Key data: 10-year Treasury rose to 5.27% from 4.9%; high-yield spreads widened to 325 basis points; triple-C corporate bonds yield ~10%. Private credit funds (Blue Owl, BDCs) limiting redemptions to 5% per quarter despite 39% withdrawal requests. Yield curve spread (102-10) at 44 basis points, below 50+ acute-stress threshold. S&P 500 earnings up 29% in three months; Moody's Analytics estimates AI drives 6-7 percentage points of inflation-adjusted GDP growth. Nasdaq-100 reached $750 target. ~$1 trillion in private credit outstanding. Kevin argues spreads reflect opportunistic reallocation rather than panic, sees valuations as compressed, and views current stress as buying opportunity, though acknowledges downside risks.
glossary.transcript_text: Credit spreads are widening. Private credit fears are growing. Does this mean we're due for a collapse? Big doom and gloom pain? Let's put some reality onto this. And so they basically limit it to 5% per quarter so they can stem the flow and they don't have to sell the underlying assets at bargain basement prices. glossary.llm_summary: Meet Kevin (YouTuber/analyst) reports Tesla Q3 2026 deliveries of 486,532 units, a 2.13% decline from Q3 2025's 497,099 but achieved without the $7,500 tax credit pull-forward that inflated 2025 figures (credit expired Sept 30, 2024). Shanghai facility delivered ~66,000 units in July (~200,000 quarterly). Speaker interprets near-parity as evidence of pricing power and demand inflection. Bullish thesis: vehicle sales remain Tesla's largest operating income driver; forecasts 4M deliveries/year by 2030 (vs ~2M now), supporting $824/share price target by end-2030 (~20% CAGR). FSD recurring revenue (~$750M/year, transitioning to ARR model) and new verticals (Optimus, Semi, Cyber Cab) contribute minority percentages. Valuation: 4.8 PEG ratio (228x forward EPS, 47% growth), elevated vs Broadcom (0.8 PEG). Key risk: Bloomberg reports Tesla risks 12% Europe market share loss if Chinese EVs gain 5% (Europe ~17% of sales); Chinese competition flagged as emerging threat to US market. Energy storage segment missed GW expectations. Macro angle: speaker forecasts peak Fed yields at 527 bps (currently 526 bps); claims if rates peak and Iran deal materializes, rate-sensitive equities like Tesla will benefit.

glossary.title: The Iran War is Flipping | Warning.
glossary.llm_summary: Meet Kevin (financial analyst/YouTuber) reports on Iran nuclear negotiations and geopolitical escalation affecting commodity and rates markets. Key facts: Iran's president and foreign minister have signaled willingness to restore IAEA weapons inspections in exchange for sanctions relief; IAEA confirmed readiness to resume inspections quickly (per CBS, Bloomberg, and economist reporting). Iranian oil exports have collapsed to less than 10% of pre-conflict levels, while Middle East exports recovered to ~17 million barrels per day (70–100% of pre-conflict), per ship-tracking data cited by The Economist. This recovery occurred despite Iran's Strait of Hormuz pressure; speaker credits US naval blockade as effective containment. US military: Trump deploying additional 9,000–10,000 troops and third carrier strike group—speaker frames this as negotiating leverage. Core thesis: Iran's economy is crumbling under blockade and sanctions, forcing capitulation; speaker forecasts nuclear deal by March 2027, bullish for markets. Nasdaq (QQQ) already hit his $750 target and will exceed $800 post-deal. Capital flows: China sold $72 billion in Treasuries over six months; Treasury yields will remain volatile until Iran deal finalizes. China forced to buy crude from open markets instead of sanctioned Iran, pushing global prices higher rather than functioning as shadow sanctions-evasion.

glossary.title: Uh Oh | The Jobs Report
glossary.llm_summary: On 2 October 2026, Meet Kevin livestreamed the US September jobs report released at 8:30 ET. Headline non-farm payrolls came in at 29,000 vs 90,000 expected—a major miss. Private payrolls: 46,000 vs 81,000 expected. Prior month revision: negative 29,000 jobs; two-month revision: negative 60,000. Average hourly earnings missed at 0.1% (expected ~0.3%) and year-over-year at 3% vs 3.1%, indicating eroding wage pressure. Household survey contrasted sharply: 485,000 jobs created. Labour force participation rose from 61.6% to 61.8%; unemployment ticked from 4.1% to 4.2%. Financial activities shed 129,000 jobs since May 2025 peak, mainly insurance carriers—attributed to AI displacement. Manufacturing up only 72,000 since December 2025 low. Temporary help employment turned negative. Speaker argues AI is destroying specific jobs (insurance underwriting, compliance) but this is masked by broader spending-driven job creation in healthcare, construction, and AI infrastructure. Market rallied: 10-year yields dropped from ~5.32% to ~5.23%; NASDAQ hit all-time highs within 5 days. Speaker contends weak report eliminates October Fed rate-hike odds and likely leaves only December cut. Thesis: labour market and AI-company viability are the two "canaries" for the bull case; once AI buildout ends and spending fades, hidden job losses will surface.

glossary.title: The Market Collapse Shock
glossary.llm_summary: Meet Kevin (financial analyst) argues that US equity market weakness—extreme breadth deterioration, equal-weight S&P 500 rolling over, financials collapsing—contradicts strong economic fundamentals. He cites Challenger Gray data showing tech layoffs remain low, September job cuts fell 18% month-over-month and 20% year-over-year. ISM manufacturing PMI reached highest since May 2022; new orders, production, and employment all growing. Lending conditions across all segments (large/mid/small firms, auto, construction) remain loose. Yet 10-year Treasury yields surged ~30bps from 4.95% (Sept 14) to 5.32% (Oct 1) despite oil prices retreating from 107–109 to ~$100. Kevin blames Japanese capital repatriation: TS Lombard data shows Japan's foreign assets fell $79.6B last month via record US Treasury sales. If Bank of Japan hikes in October while Fed stays pat, yield spread widens, accelerating repatriation. GPU rental prices (H100/H200) are rising despite 50%+ of token spend in openweight models—AI boom remains robust. Kevin forecasts 10-year peak near 5.27%, Iran deal closure by election (90–95% confidence), and once both constraints lift, NASDAQ 100 rallies to 800+ by year-end. He notes 16 prior Treasury rallies of this magnitude preceded dislocations (1987, 2018, 2008, SVB) but argues underlying AI capex and economic growth will prevail once geopolitical and capital-flow headwinds clear.

Examples cite Warren Buffett (minimal salary, wealth via stock appreciation) and Elon Musk (borrowing against Tesla stock). Contains a sponsored health-litigation segment. No data on macro conditions, commodity prices, currency markets, geopolitics, China, or Australian equities.

glossary.llm_summary: Meet Kevin argues that a fundamental Fed regime change under Kevin Worsh—explicitly anti-money printing, preferring negative rates over QE—will reshape investment returns over the next 8–10 years. Current bond yields (10-year 5.28%, 2-year ~4.9–5%) are driven primarily by oil prices and Middle East geopolitical risk, not fiscal crisis (per TS Lombard). An Iran deal is expected soon, potentially marking peak yields. In the event of recession, the Fed will not run the money printer; instead, it will pursue austerity or negative rates. This regime benefits bonds (especially held to maturity) and real estate in supply-constrained jurisdictions through falling long-term rates and historically low mortgage rates. Gold will underperform, as this is an 'anti-gold Fed.' The AI bubble remains in early-to-mid cycle, with the labor market as the key canary for recession onset. The speaker forecasts a deflationary downturn within the next decade (likely by 2032), after which capital flows will shift from equities to bonds and real estate. Kevin Worsh's stated anti-inflation posture and the composition of his task force suggest a multi-year tightening bias, even in a crisis.

glossary.llm_summary: Meet Kevin analyzes US-Iran negotiations through an energy and macro lens. Key data: US crude inventories dropped to 922k barrels (vs 2.9M prior); three tankers attacked in Strait of Hormuz Tuesday; crude flows at 17.5M bbl/day (98% pre-war), refined products 3M bbl/day (58% pre-war). Iran demands frozen funds ($12B in Qatar), sanctions lift, maritime blockade removal before negotiating Hormuz opening; US demands nuclear inspections first, then Strait opening. Betting markets show 32% probability of nuclear deal by March 1, 2027. Economically: ADP employment came in at 90k (expected 75k), but financial services and professional/business services lost 27k jobs combined. Chicago PMI at strongest pace since May. PCE inflation beat expectations: 0.2% monthly (expected 0.3%), 3% annual core (expected 3.3%). Fed's Williams signals no October rate hike; Treasury Secretary Yellen announces $6B buyback for 10-20 year bonds October 1. Speaker interprets Trump's negotiation posture as deliberately slow, maintaining SPR drawdown to signal strength while Iran currency weakens.

glossary.llm_summary: A FlyDubai 737 Max flight (FZ1073, A6-FKF) en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv underwent an extreme emergency descent on 30 September, descending from 34,000 ft to ~16,600 ft in approximately 1 minute at a descent rate of ~17,000 ft/min—well exceeding structural limits (300–320 ft/min). The squawk code was changed from 7700 (general emergency) to 7500 (hijacking). According to Israeli security reports, one of the two pilots (allegedly an Omani pilot) attempted to stab the other (allegedly Emirati) and possibly hijack the plane, potentially to crash it. Passengers near the cockpit and two off-duty pilots on board restrained the attacker; both pilots were injured and treated. The aircraft diverted to Saudi Arabia and landed successfully with a torn rudder; no fatalities reported. Israel's air force scrambled fighter jets. The incident is framed by Israeli officials as a potential act of terrorism. The speaker, a commercial jet pilot, notes it is extraordinary the aircraft did not structurally fail given the extreme descent rate and associated aerodynamic stresses.

glossary.llm_summary: Felix Prehn argues that recent scary economic headlines mask bullish signals for equities. Oil has risen 50% to ~$100/barrel over the past year, with the US now the world's largest producer (66% above Saudi Arabia, 70% above Russia, nearly 3x 2008 levels). This structural reversal means high prices now benefit rather than cost the American economy. US real estate job openings collapsed from 95,000 to 50,000 between July and August 2026, the lowest level since 2024. Prehn argues this slowdown signals the Federal Reserve will pause rate hikes and potentially cut rates in coming months. Despite elevated bearishness—48% of American investors expect lower stock market returns within 6 months versus a 31% historical average—Prehn invokes a contrarian pattern: when investor bearishness reaches such extremes, markets have historically rallied. In 2009 (70% bearish) the S&P 500 rose 67% over 12 months; in 2022 (60% bearish) it rose 18%. The M2 money supply expanded by nearly $1 trillion in 2026 versus $600 billion in 2025, the fastest pace since 2022, signalling future liquidity support. However, 82% of S&P 500 stocks are down despite the index rising 13%, indicating extreme concentration. Prehn contends money now follows quality companies with growing revenues and earnings rather than broad index diversification.

glossary.title: If You Don't Pay a Dividend, You're Not in Business (Tony Kiernan)
glossary.llm_summary: Interview with Tony Kiernan, Western Australian lawyer-turned-mining executive with 20+ years chairing major resources companies, published 2026-09-30. Interview focuses on career philosophy and principles rather than current market analysis. Kiernan chairs or chaired: BCI Iron (iron ore miner, listed ~$12m, achieved production independence via FMG rail access agreement despite conceding project value; declared first dividend after building mine and reaching port); Pilgrim Minerals (lithium explorer to ASX 50 producer; when Kiernan joined ~2016 valued ~$500m with no mine; subsequently listed Brinsfield mine and acquired Alura project; current MD Dale Henderson describes lithium as experiencing 'winter' and 'summer' price cycles); Northern Star (via Saracen board, which acquired 50% of Superpit); Genesis (gold: from ~$300m to >$8bn market cap during his tenure from 2022; merging with Vault, Kiernan becoming deputy chair); Chalice (Eritrea gold project, open-pit ore at 5g/t grade, sold to Chinese consortium after facing institutional resistance due to geopolitical risk). Kiernan articulates three core rules for commodity mining: (1) price-taker status—producers cannot influence commodity prices; (2) inherently risk business—combining general business risk with nature/geopolitical risk; (3) don't live the dream (commodity prices collapse quickly). Business philosophy centers on: cost control as only controllable lever; balance sheet fortress (maintained $90m+ cash buffer for Genesis contingency); dividend discipline; disciplined capital allocation. During lithium expansion, conventional banks refused to finance lithium projects; Pilgrim accessed Nordic bond markets instead. Raises concerns about Australian regulatory framework inadequacies and political misunderstanding of mining's importance to national revenue.

glossary.llm_summary: Meet Kevin discusses whether recent surges in AMD (up 183% YTD) and Intel (up 214% YTD) stocks are justified by actual agentic AI CPU demand. He cites Vicram Seeker's analysis that one AMD Venice 256-core chip can support ~896 agent instances through shared CPU resources. Assuming 10M active agents by end-2026 growing 100x to 1B by 2030, he calculates total CPU revenue at ~$5.5B (2027–2030)—negligible versus Nvidia's $90–100B quarterly datacenter revenue. He argues the CPU trade is overblown; agents can run on $417 mini PCs or even iPhones (which offer 3x better memory bandwidth); memory, not CPU, is the real constraint. Frontier AI (anthropic, OpenAI) is where profit concentrates, not edge CPUs.

glossary.title: Why the Oil Crisis Is (Secretly) Good...
glossary.llm_summary: Strait of Hormuz oil crisis framed as asymmetric US advantage. US is world's largest oil producer and LNG exporter — benefits from supply tightness. Asia (China, India, Japan, South Korea) takes 75% of Persian Gulf oil and faces supply disruption risk. Geopolitical angle: Hormuz disruption as US leverage in US-China trade negotiations. Indirectly bullish for gold via USD strength and geopolitical uncertainty, but no direct gold analysis.
glossary.transcript_text: Right now, the world thinks it's watching an oil crisis unfold. And on the surface, it makes sense why. Because energy markets are all over the place, and governments across Europe and Asia are scrambling to hold emergency meetings. And all of the panic can be traced back to one place, the straight of Hormuz, a narrow strip of water that provides the only sea passage from the Persian Gulf to the open ocean. And every single day, roughly 20% of the world's oil passes through it, which makes it the single most important choke point on the planet. And the general consensus is pretty clear. If something goes wrong here, the global economy is totally But maybe that's just the story we're being told. And maybe it's only half the story, because the truth is there's a lot more going on here. Because the real story isn't just about what's happening. It's about who it's happening to. Because oil shocks don't hit the world equally, and they never have. Because while some economies get crushed, others quietly benefit. And that's what this story is really about. It's not a story about a crisis. It's about positioning. Because most people still think this plays out like it did 20 years ago where instability in the Middle East leads to an oil shock which eventually hits the US economy. And for a long time, this was true because 20 years ago, the United States was heavily dependent on foreign oil. In fact, roughly 60% of the total petroleum consumption was from imports. So when the global supply got disrupted, the impact was immediate. Prices spiked, inflation surged, and the economy hit pause. It was a clear linear relationship. But that version of the world doesn't exist anymore. Because over the past two decades, something changed. New drilling techniques unlocked massive shale reserves for the United States. And production boomed. And suddenly, the United States didn't just reduce its dependence on foreign oil, it flipped the entire script. Because if you fast forward to the present, the United States is the largest oil producer in the world. Which means the old narrative, it's outdated because now the United States isn't on the same side of the trade anymore. So now the question becomes then who actually is exposed? And this is where you get to the real story because most of the oil moving through the straight of Hormuz isn't going to the United States. In fact, only 2 and 12% of it is. The majority of the oil in the Middle East is going somewhere else to Asia and more specifically China, India, Japan, and South Korea. Because together, these four countries account for roughly 75% of all the oil moving through the straight. So when people say a disruption here will shock the global economy, they're not wrong. But they're also missing something very important. It's an asymmetric shock. And it doesn't hit everyone equally. Because for the United States, a disruption mostly just becomes a price problem. And that's because oil is globally priced. So if supply tightens anywhere, oil prices rise all over, which hurts. But it's at least manageable. But for Asia, it's different because it isn't just a price problem. It also becomes a supply problem. And those are very different things because higher prices slow you down. But losing access to your energy supply, well, that's when things can start to break. Where factories slow, energy gets rationed, and production stalls. It's the same event, but with completely different consequences. And this is where the story shifts from crisis to positioning because when supply tightens and prices rise, it creates winners and losers. And right now, the United States is on the winning side because higher prices don't just hurt. It also generates revenue for producers, for exporters, and for energy companies. And the United States just happens to be the world's largest oil producer, which means the same shock that's creating global pain is also stimulating parts of the US economy. But oil is also only half the story because there's a second layer that most people are completely overlooking. Natural gas. Because the Middle East is also one of the largest exporters of liqufied natural gas in the world. And just like oil, a massive portion of it flows through the straight of Hormuz. In fact, it's roughly 20% of the global supply of liqufied natural gas. And countries like Qatar and the United Arab Emirates send over 90% of their liqufied natural gas exports through the strait. So if the straight gets disrupted, it's not just the oil markets that tighten, it's gas markets, too. And once again, this is where the United States shows up. Because over the past decade, the United States has quietly become the largest exporter of liqufied natural gas in the world, which means the same dynamic repeats. One region loses supply and another steps in to sell it. And the markets are already beginning to react to this, which is why we're seeing energy companies rise and exporters benefit. Venture Global, one of the fastest growing LNG exporters, has seen its stock jump nearly 40% in the past month. And Chener Energy, the largest LNG exporter in the US, is up nearly 15%. And on the crude oil side, we're seeing the same thing. And that's because scarcity doesn't just create risk, it creates opportunity. glossary.title: How Capital Cycles Create 100 Baggers In Plain Sight
glossary.llm_summary: Django Davidson interview on capital cycle investing framework applied to mining. Framework origin: Jeremy Grantham/GMO 1990s — supply is measurable, demand is storytelling; focus on supply constraints. Codified in Edward Chancellor's book 'Capital Account' (out of print, ~$2,000 on eBay). Core principle: long-run share price is driven by return on capital, not earnings. Industries with declining returns on capital (hyperscalers spending $700B on data centers, OpenAI offering 17.5% guaranteed returns to PE) will disappoint. Industries with rising returns (constrained supply, no new capacity being built) will compound. Incentives drive booms: promoters raise $1 → market values at $3-10 → fee networks of banks, intermediaries sustain momentum. Capital cycle as contrarian guard rails: avoid mass capacity addition + IPO boom (correctly warned on lithium). Look for bust-phase industries where no new supply being built. Rick Rule quoted: 'if you're not a contrarian you're going to be a victim.' Applied to ASX mining: lithium avoided on supply glut; beaten-down mining sectors with rising returns on capital now at sweet spot of capital cycle. The key behavioral edge: as prices rise, investor returns on capital definitionally fall — yet animal spirits make investors more enthusiastic at exactly the wrong time.

glossary.llm_summary: Mechanistic explanation for why gold falls during geopolitical crises before rallying sharply. Oil spike → inflation expectations rise → Fed cannot cut rates → bond yields rise (US 10y competing at ~5%) → dollar strengthens → three simultaneous headwinds crush gold. Historical pattern validated across every major oil shock: 1973 OPEC embargo (gold +150% over 2 years, +2300% 1971-1980 full period); 1979 Iranian Revolution (+89% next 12 months); 1991 Gulf War (+10% pop); post-9/11 ($250→$1,900 decade bull run); 2022 Ukraine (broke $2,000). Four-phase recovery: Phase 1 (week 1-4 panic); Phase 2 (month 2-3 gold drops 15-20%, retail capitulates — worst time to sell); Phase 3 (month 4-18, structural bid returns, miners lever up); Phase 4 (month 12+, new all-time highs). Current setup more extreme than any prior oil shock: $38T US debt, 1,000+ tons/yr central bank buying, three-year silver supply deficit, institutional smart money at extreme short — historically precedes large rallies. Five sector outperformers during crises: gold miners (GDX, 2-3x leverage to gold), silver (SLV), energy (XLE, Strait of Hormuz = 20% of world oil), defense (ITA, +47% vs S&P post-9/11), utilities (XLU, flat in 2022 when S&P -15%).

glossary.llm_summary: US military posture in the Iran war is shifting from air power to ground-option readiness. Two Marine Expeditionary Units (~4,400 troops) deployed to the Persian Gulf. Escalation spectrum analyzed: special forces raids on nuclear stockpile (Isfahan/Fordow) or missile factories; limited territorial seizures of Strait of Hormuz islands (Kish, Qeshm, Abu Musa, Greater/Lesser Tumb) and Kharg Island oil infrastructure; full-scale invasion requiring 200,000+ troops assessed as strategic disaster comparable to Iraq but harder. Key asymmetry: Iran only needs to survive each day while US needs decisive victory. IRGC is decentralized (31 autonomous brigades), so leadership decapitation has limited effect. Amphibious assault on defended coastline last attempted in Korea 1950. Bottom line: ground operations remain possible but each step escalates political and military costs exponentially; rivals (Russia, China) exploit US distraction in other theaters.

US air strikes may damage some of these sites, but the network itself is designed to survive bombardment through redundancy and mobility. seizing or disabling key positions, particularly the islands of Abu Musa, Greater Tumb and Lesser Tumb, and the coastal bases near Bandar Abbas could temporarily weaken Thran's ability to interfere with one of the world's most important energy corridors. That is exactly the type of mission marine expeditionary units are built to carry out. Another potential objective would be Iran's oil export infrastructure. Car Island, which handles the overwhelming majority of the country's crude shipments, has already been struck by American air power. US forces recently destroyed dozens of military installations on the island, targeting missile storage sites and naval mine facilities. But the energy infrastructure itself was deliberately left intact. That restraint leaves Washington with a powerful escalation option. If the war continues to widen, Trump could still choose to Iran's export hub, either through further air strikes or by temporarily seizing the island. Beyond that, even more ambitious options have recently come into view. American forces could attempt to seize a major port such as Bander Abbas or Chabahar, both of which are vital to Iran's maritime trade. Even the threat of a landing near large coastal cities could force Thran to divert military forces away from other parts of the conflict. But amphibious assaults are among the most difficult operations in warfare. The United States has conducted landings in places like Panama in 1989, Beirut in 1958, and Haiti in 1994. But these were unopposed landings, meaning they were conducted without hostile fire. The last time America attempted a truly contested landing against a defended coastline was during the Korean War in 1950. Doing so today would expose landing forces to drones, anti-ship missiles, coastal defenses, and artillery. Even if the initial assault succeeded, American troops could quickly find themselves fighting in dense urban areas where many of their technological advantages begin to fade. Moreover, the geography and distance of such an operation favor. Iranian forces would be operating close to their own bases, supply lines, and missile systems, while American troops would depend on ships and regional bases that could themselves become targets. For that reason, focusing on Iran's isolated islands is a far more manageable objective than the large coastal cities. Yet, perhaps the hardest question of all is what happens after. Capturing territory is one thing. holding it and eventually getting out is something else entirely. The final option, and the most dramatic one, would be a full-scale invasion, one aimed either at dismantling Iran's conventional military forces or bringing down the Islamic Republic altogether. But an operation of this scale would come at an enormous cost. For comparison, the invasion of Iraq in 2003 required more than 6 months to assemble around 200,000 soldiers in the region. Iran, however, is larger in size and population and is more mountainous. So, the required number of troops and resources would be many times that of the Iraqi experience. The United States would also need regional support. Neighboring countries would have to host American troops and allow supply lines to run through their territory. Yet few governments appear to have an appetite for total war. Then there is the political challenge at home. A war of this scale would require massive funding and long-term commitment. Under US law, Congress would almost certainly need to approve such an operation. Without broad public support, sustaining a prolonged ground war would be extremely difficult. Fortunately, we're not there yet. A full-scale invasion is unlikely. Only a major economic or military blow from Iran would be enough to push public opinion toward a ground war. Assuming that obstacles such as funding, mobilization, popular support, and regional logistics were overcome, Washington could then begin assembling the forces required for a fullscale invasion. This would likely involve a buildup of hundreds of thousands of troops with the initial phase focusing on amphibious landings along Iran's southern coast and a push toward major cities and the oilrich province of Kuzan. American forces could then attempt to weaken the Iranian military while supporting local opposition groups, similar to the strategy used in Afghanistan in 2001. or they might attempt a direct advance toward Thran as they did with Baghdad 2 years later. Either way, a full-scale invasion of Iran would be nothing short of a strategic disaster. There would be no quick victory. It would likely unfold over months or years, especially if the United States relied on proxy forces rather than committing to a direct advance into the Iranian interior. And even then, victory on the battlefield would only mark the beginning of a far longer phase. Iran's population is large, its terrain is difficult, and stabilizing the country could tie down American forces for years, if not decades. All it would do is drain American resources away from Europe and Asia. And when a superpower is busy in one theater, its rivals rehearse in another. I've been your host Shervan from Caspian Report. glossary.title: Forget FalconBridge. NexGen is Gilman's Big Score
glossary.llm_summary: Warren Gilman career story focused on his Hong Kong years and NexGen Energy's Arrow uranium deposit. Key narrative: moved to Hong Kong 1999 (escaped Perth during gold's $200 bottom) → became the only mining expert working with Lee Ka-shing during China's commodity supercycle emergence → worked on landmark deals including MinMetals/Falconbridge, Placer+Barrick merger, Meridian Gold IPO. In Hong Kong in 2005-2007: China's MinMetals, Jinchuan, Zin were leading international mining M&A. Pattern recognized: large, world-class ore bodies almost inevitably end up in major integrated miners' portfolios. NexGen's Arrow deposit (Athabasca Basin) just received final permits after 10 years — Lee Ka-shing cornerstone investor via $60M convertible arranged by cold call 10 years ago. Iran war as direct uranium demand catalyst: parallels 1973 Arab oil embargo which sparked a decade of nuclear buildout for energy security. BHP/Rio historically reluctant on uranium despite Olympic Dam, but oil companies (BP once owned copper/gold/lime mines via Selection Trust acquisition) may return to mining for nuclear feedstock. Energy security imperative now more acute than any time since 1973.

glossary.title: What Gold’s Past Tells Us About Its Future
glossary.llm_summary: Interview with Sean (Australian gold corporate historian) on the current gold mining bull market. Sean started in the industry in 1984 — in the shadow of the 1980 $850 gold peak. Key historical pattern: gold stocks lagged the 1980 gold price spike (investors were too panicked to buy equities), then boomed in 1986-87 on relative multiple expansion — not DCF justification, just EV-per-resource-ounce comparisons. Analogy: similar to dot-com era where earnings multiples were meaningless but relative multiples still drove markets. Current bull market: gold stocks hottest in years, but generalists not yet in. Institutional threshold effect: when stocks cross $1B market cap, pension funds can invest regardless of insider valuation concerns — once this happens, momentum accelerates and insiders feel valuations are 'nuts' but stocks keep going. Narrative follows price (Michael Cheney: 'none of the people telling you where it's going predicted the boom'). Charts and ratios (gold stocks vs gold price, gold vs S&P) more useful than fundamentals for timing cyclical tops. Capital must flow somewhere — gold is a natural destination when money supply expands. New Zealand gold region (Enduro-associated consolidation play) highlighted as exciting. Strong view: current setup could develop into one of the greatest gold equity bull markets in history if generalist capital finally rotates in.

glossary.title: Why Aluminium Just Went Vertical
glossary.llm_summary: Deep dive into aluminium supply chain dynamics. Rule of thumb: 5 tons bauxite → 2 tons alumina → 1 ton primary aluminium. 2024-2025 alumina price spike caused by converging shocks: Quinana refinery shutdown (Queensland), Rio Tinto force majeure on Queensland gas supply, Brazilian refinery disruption, Guinea bauxite disruptions (world's largest non-China bauxite source). China Yunnan hydro power adequate in 2025, preventing smelting cuts. Result: alumina price spike then collapse — now ~40% of global alumina refining sector loss-making (below cost curve). Primary aluminium price performing well due to: China 45M ton smelting capacity cap (no new capacity), strong demand (EVs, construction), tariff speculation on US imports. Debate on integrated vs non-integrated model (Rio Tinto): historically vertically integrated gave stability through cycle, but spot bauxite/alumina markets now viable. ASX relevance: Rio Tinto's aluminium division (bauxite in QLD, alumina at Yarwun/QAL, smelting at Tomago/Portland) directly affected. Aluminium demand slow-burn growth — world needs at least one new smelter per year indefinitely.

glossary.llm_summary: Leon from Arrakis Global — generalist macro fund manager — discusses investment philosophy and commodity themes. Core philosophy: don't lose money, cut positions at 2% drawdown, maximum cognitive flexibility across asset classes. Process evolution from fundamental to incorporating momentum, market structure, narrative + price action as fluid interacting system. Key current themes: European defense (paradigm shift confirmed by Trump-Vance Munich Security Conference + Zelensky White House moment — thesis: JD Vance lecturing European leaders = fundamental NATO commitment shift); commodities via 'rolling crackup' supply constraint thesis. Each commodity hits its shortage wall independently (TTF gas 2021, LME nickel 2022, oil Ukraine 2022, uranium 2023, copper 2024 fits/starts). Now seeing rare convergence where all commodities moving together on the same days — possibly Rolling Crackup thesis merging with India emerging demand + dollar debasement narrative. AI data center boom exhibits classic bubble misallocation signals: OpenAI offering guaranteed 17.5% returns to PE, massive fee networks sustaining momentum. Contrasts with commodity markets where forcing function (someone needs delivery tomorrow, price-inelastic) rewards active research over passive allocation.

Three layers of Australian energy market: macro oil (geopolitical, Iran war → oil $70→$90+); macro LNG (global, still young market); domestic gas (parochial, policy-driven, east coast reservation policies). Background: 2007-2014 boom followed by 2014-2020 bust (ESG pressure + COVID oversupply). ESG headwinds now fading, funding returning. Iran war: every $10 oil rise costs import-dependent countries $4-5B/yr extra. Key ASX names benefiting from higher energy prices and policy chaos: Woodside (LNG), APA Group (domestic gas infrastructure). Australian east coast domestic gas market subject to extreme policy risk which creates volatility = trading opportunity.

glossary.title: The New Commodity Supercycle Is Already Here (Paulo Macro)
glossary.llm_summary: Paulo Macro presents thesis that the commodity supercycle is underway but structurally different from the 2000s China demand-pull boom. In 2000s: $300B AUM flooded commodities on China demand — topped 2011, then 10+ years underinvestment. Current cycle: supply-constrained, not demand-pulled. Rolling crackups: individual commodities hit shortage walls sequentially rather than all rising together — European TTF gas (fall 2021), LME nickel $80,000/t (Feb 2022, trades busted), oil $120 on Ukraine invasion, uranium $100+ (2023), copper (2024 fits/starts). Key insight: 'forcing function' in commodities (someone needs delivery tomorrow, price-inelastic) rewards active research unlike fixed income (Fed-watching) and equities (passive/buybacks = momentum). Dollar has strengthened 10 years (suppressing EM demand) but Trump debasement narrative now kicking — India GDP per capita hitting S-curve for commodity-intensive growth. Signs emerging that all commodities moving together again like 2000s (energy + metals + uranium + gold correlating) — possible convergence of Rolling Crackup + India demand + debasement. Capital cycle guard rails: warned on lithium (correctly) — mass capacity addition + IPO boom = supply glut. Platinum: up 60% in 3 months after 12 months flat (patience rewarded). Contrarian + capital cycle discipline = less bad decisions.
glossary.transcript_text: My bigger takeaway was how unsynchronized the global economy seems to be now in terms of where we are in the cycle. Usually it's you know US catches a cold the rest of the world gets the flu maybe with a lag. I don't know if that's true this time because Hong Kong and China seem to be in flecting off the lows. Hello Macro. Thank you so much for for joining us again mate. It's been a while since we last spoke and there has been heaps happening in the world of of metals and mining and markets more broadly. One of the one of the big themes that I'm keen to jump into first is your idea of the the present super cycle we're in and how that kind of contrasts with the China bull market that we saw in the 2000s where you really sort of cut your teeth in. So, I'd love to kind of start right there and and hear your your evolution on thinking in this this super cycle, the the rolling crackups thesis that you have and and everything related. >> Oh, wow. Um, well, first off, thanks fellas for uh having me back. Um, I guess it's I can't believe a year has gone by if I think it's been a year. And uh I um I I I'm sorry. I know you guys have been reaching out for uh for a while now to um to have me back and it's uh I've just been completely snowed. uh as I think you boys like to say, although it never snows in Australia, so I don't know why you guys say it, but uh um you're taking me way back. Uh this is kind of one of my first framework notes when I first moved to Substack. So it's um it's like really big picture how I think about the world in comparing today or more like comparing and contrasting today versus the 2000s. Um so happy to jump in right there. I think for me in starting out in the 2000s especially with a commodity bent um as a kind of a young bloke starting in the business and actually uh one of my first assignments was Australian equities. So I've got a very soft sweet spot in my heart for uh you boys down under um and been there many times and uh in my 20s starting out the cycle was just getting going. But there were a couple of key points that were different then versus today. Um for one you had a very clear demand pull uh from the emerging China. We all know that story. But uh that kind of measure of a rise a rising tide lifting all boats uh did some interesting things to a space that had been mostly cast aside for you know the better part of uh 20 plus years. Um going back all the way to the 70s which was kind of our last big commodity secular bull. Um, in this case with China's coming out party after the WTO and the rise of China uh and Chinese demand hitting that kind of scurve of GDP per capita that a lot of people talk about when they think about global south, India and Southeast Asia today. You had a situation where two things happened at once. You had that kind of general demand pull where the entire demand curve pushes out and to the right. And you also had an interesting exercise come out, I believe around 2004, where McKenzie dropped a a a research note uh report uh arguing that if you took your typical equity and bond uh fixed uh uh fixed income allocation uh and added a passive commodity exposure via futures to those two uh even around the edges. Uh what they found was two amazing things. one, the returns from commodities historically were uncorrelated uh near zero to either of those asset classes. So it made sense as a bolt-on to 60/40 and more importantly that as all of these curves which naturally want to sit in contango, if you want to store a commodity, you need a contango where the near-term price is cheaper to the fartherdated price to pay for shipping, storage, in particular storage and insurance. Then as you backwardate, which is the curve's way of punishing stores and calling supplies out to the market, you passively begin to collect a yield. So you were basically ringing the dinner bell for pension fund allocators who were looking for other options. And remember this is in the early mid 2000s when hedge funds and alternatives were just starting to get going. So, you know, hedge funds were in an allocatable asset class the way private equity and credit is today among universities where 40% of their their billion-dollar endowments are in in privates. Back then, it was really stocks and bonds and a little around the edges and the David Swinson Yale University CIOS of the world were playing with alternatives uh around the edges, but the mass market kind of longdated saver, insurance companies, pensions, what have you, were only starting to wake up to this. This McKenzie report woke people up to the fact that you had non-correlated A and positive ruled yield B. And if you basically tell somebody that you have an uncorrelated asset class that generates a positive yield in an environment like the early mid200s when the Fed had cut to 1% and basically kicked off the real estate bubble in the US. That was like ringing the dinner bell for large allocators. And so commodities rose as an asset class and we saw $300 billion of AUM flood into the space during that boom in the 2000s which all of course uh was you know miraculously crowned and ended with the demise of Lehman Brothers and the financial crisis in08. There was a an echo boom coming out of that but by 2011 that was the ultimate top of commodities and emerging markets and we were done. The difference this time uh kind of setting the table with that is you don't have a very clear uh demand pull in one particular place per se. Uh the dollar has been gradually strengthening for 10 years which has kind of been a boot on the neck of EM since 2011 as we know. Um more recently Trump seems to want to change that. The debasement trade is underway. It's starting to catch fire as a longer term narrative. Weaker dollar will you know be a kick in the butt for emerging market demand. uh that's all great and maybe India owns the second half of the 2020s or the 2030s uh and some of these economies very large are hitting their S- curves now you know as they kick through 2500 $3,000 GDP per capita but the real driver so far of commodities has been the supply constraint that followed the boom uh where basically the tide went out for 10 plus years uh uh via underinvestment and that underinvestment shifts the supply curve in as opposed to the China story which pushed the demand curve out. The outcome is the same. You get a general appreciation starting in the price level, but it reflects in the market in a different way. Whereas the backward dating curves driven by China is a rising tide that lifts pretty much all commodity boats at around the same time. Here what we're seeing is different commodities run into the wall of shortage or you know a production crack up or a slip up at different points in time which actually is Christmas for an active commodity manager or someone who uh wants to take a longer short you know active approach and I I call this also the forcing function in commodities they seem to do nothing for a long time and then suddenly they'll work 50% out of nowhere over a few weeks or months and that forcing function in commodities is expressed because someone has a problem somewhere or needs delivery tomorrow. glossary.llm_summary: Iran war is being determined by three pressure points: munitions, markets, and midterms.
