glossary.transcript_text: People often imagine armed conflicts being won or lost on the battlefield. Armies advance, enemies retreat, and eventually one side wins. But modern wars rarely end that way. They end when three things start breaking at the same time. Munitions, markets, and midterms. These pressure points determine how long hostilities can realistically continue. In the first 5 days of this war, the United States burned through roughly 800 Patriot interceptors. Once munitions begin to run low, commanders must face difficult choices. They can either slow the pace of operations or redeploy assets from elsewhere. The Pentagon has opted for the latter. It is cannibalizing missile systems across Asia-Pacific to sustain combat operations. This video shows six THAD launchers being removed from the US base in South Korea and being redeployed to the Middle East. Markets, however, don't care about battlefield victories. They're concerned with stability. If investors believe a conflict might escalate into a prolonged crisis, they begin preparing for the economic consequences long before those consequences fully appear. Data centers shut down. Shipping companies change routes, capital starts moving towards safer assets and so on. The closing of the straight of Hormuz, for instance, doesn't just affect fuel prices. It ripples through freight, food, housing, and even water infrastructure. Modern life rests on stable energy flows. And once those begin to fluctuate, the effects spread outward. So while military planners focus on operational objectives, political leaders must also consider how the conflict is upsetting inflation, energy prices, and the broader economy. Even superpowers must negotiate with reality. We may be living in what feels like the most anxietyinducing era in recent memory. Not necessarily the most dangerous period in history, but one that often feels that way. Between alarming headlines, endless commentary, and the temptation to keep doom scrolling, it's easy to feel overwhelmed by everything happening around us. I caught myself in that spiral recently, just scrolling through updates late at night, one headline after another. At some point, you're no longer staying informed. You're just feeding the anxiety. One thing that can help is simply having space to step back and process it all. For many people, therapy provides that space, a chance to reflect, gain perspective, and better understand the patterns shaping how we think and respond to stress. BetterHelp, the sponsor of today's episode, makes it easier to start therapy. You can take a short quiz and get matched with a credentialed therapist and you can communicate in the way that works best for you, whether by phone, video, or text. And if the match isn't right, you can switch therapists at any time at no extra cost. More than 6 million people have already gotten help through BetterHelp. If you're interested, click the link in the description or go to betterhelp.com/caspianreport to get 10% off your first month of therapy. The first pressure point in modern warfare is munitions. Everything hinges on this. At first glance, the US military appears almost limitless in firepower. Precision missiles can strike targets hundreds of kilometers away. Satellites track movements in real time, while air defense systems intercept rockets mid-flight. It almost looks as if advanced militaries can simply keep fighting for as long as they want. But there is a quiet reality behind all of this. Modern weapons are extraordinarily difficult to produce. A Tomahawk missile is not just a metal tube filled with explosives. It contains specialized electronics, advanced guidance systems, and components that come from long supply chains. Many of those parts are produced in small quantities by only a handful of manufacturers. The same is true for interceptor missiles, long range drones, and precisiong guided bombs, which means these weapons cannot be replaced quickly. At the start of a conflict, this problem is easy to miss. Militaries rely on stockpiles built up over years. Those reserves allow them to sustain a high tempo of strikes in the early stages of a war. Missiles fly, air defenses intercept, and so commanders operate as if supply is not an issue. But stockpiles don't last forever, and once they begin to shrink, the war starts to run into industrial constraints. Factories cannot scale production overnight. Doing so would require time, skilled labor, and above all, multi-year contracts with suppliers. Take the SM3 interceptor missile as an example. The US Navy uses it to shoot down ballistic missiles. Depending on the variant, each missile costs roughly 10 to 28 million. That price tag reflects its complexity. The missile must detect a ballistic warhead in space, track it, and collide with it at several kilometers/s using a kinetic kill vehicle. It's essentially a small spacecraft designed to destroy another object traveling faster than a bullet. But because of that complexity, the production of SM3 missiles is limited. The exact number is classified, but they're produced in relatively small batches. often only dozens per year depending on the Pentagon's procurements. Another example is the Patriot Pack 3 Interceptor, one of the main missiles used by America and Israel to shoot down Iranian missiles. Each Pac 3 interceptor costs roughly 4 to 5 million. However, in spite of its widespread use, production is relatively limited. In 2025, manufacturer Loheed Martin produced around 620 PAC 3 interceptors. That seems plenty at first, but modern air defense systems often fire multiple interceptors at a single incoming missile to ensure a successful kill. In a prolonged highintensity conflict, this equation gradually shifts the nature of the war. One night of missile defense can burn through months of production. This video shows over a dozen Patriot interceptors launched from the local US air base during an Iranian missile barrage. That's about 2% of the Patriots annual production gone in under a minute. No war machine runs this hot forever. The same munitions constraint exists on the Iranian side, though it looks very different. Iran possesses one of the largest ballistic missile arsenals in the Middle East, estimated at several thousand. But missiles alone do not determine how much firepower a country can bring to the battlefield. They also need launchers. These launch vehicles must constantly move, hide, and reposition. The moment a missile is fired, sensors and satellites can often trace the launch back to its origin, making the vehicle itself a prime target. Destroy enough of these launchers, and even a large missile stockpile becomes useless. Iran has also invested heavily in drones, which push the economics of war even further. Systems like the Shahed 136 are rudimentary when compared to missiles, but they're built with small engines and basic electronics and are estimated to cost between 20 and $50,000 each with some estimates going as low as 7,000. Launched in waves, these drones force defenders to spend far more expensive interceptors, gradually saturating air defenses and exhausting stockpiles faster than they can be replenished. Altogether, these dynamics show that modern warfare depends as much on industry as on tactics. Victory belongs to the side that can sustain the flow of weapons. Armed conflicts today face another pressure point that did not exist to the same degree in the past. Financial markets. The moment fighting breaks out in a strategically important region, energy prices move within hours. Transportation costs rise and investors start reassessing risks. Often times, these market fluctuations happen long before governments decide how to respond. We're already seeing this dynamic unfold. Oil prices jumped as soon as hostilities began to disrupt traffic near the straight of Hormuz. Governments moved quickly to calm markets by releasing strategic reserves and signaling that additional supplies could be brought online if needed. Those measures helped stabilize prices for the moment. But the episode illustrates how sensitive global markets are. And this is not just about oil. Once energy markets begin moving, the effects trickle down. Freight becomes more expensive, manufacturing costs rise, and inflation begins creeping upward again. All these disruptions move far faster than military campaigns, and they ripple through global supply chains. Fertilizer production, for example, depends heavily on natural gas. When energy prices rise, the cost of producing ammonia, the key ingredient in nitrogen fertilizers, rises as well. That increase eventually reaches farmers, which months from now raises the cost of staple crops such as wheat, corn, and rice. Global aviation is another example. The Middle East sits at the crossroads of major air routts connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa. About 2/3 of the global population lives within an 8-hour flight of Doha and Dubai. So when missiles, drones, or air defense systems threaten regional airspace, carriers are forced to reroute flights around the danger zones. This is how the region's airspace looks right now. Azerbaijan is effectively the single direct link between Europe and Asia. But it's more than just that. The trickle down consequences don't necessarily stay local. Distant sectors feel them too. Much of the recent momentum in the American stock market and a hefty portion of US economic growth is driven by a handful of tech giants, often referred to as the Magnificent 7. These companies dominate the market. In 2023 alone, they accounted for around 60% of the SNP500's total return, which goes to show just how concentrated the market rally has become. However, the expansion of these tech giants depends on massive investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure, particularly the data centers that power cloud computing and machine learning. The UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Bahrain have been actively courting these tech giants to host regional cloud and AI hubs in an effort to position themselves as digital infrastructure centers. But Iran treats this digital infrastructure as part of the conflict itself. Iranian drones have already damaged Amazon data centers in the UAE and Bahrain which have disrupted cloud services used by banks and companies in the region. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia, IBM, Oracle and Palanteer are now all legitimate targets according to the IRGC. By threatening or damaging the overseas infrastructure of these firms, Iran is attempting to hurt the digital backbone of the American tech sector and by extension a key engine of US economic growth. Pipelines, shipping, fertilizers, data centers. That's just the start. The ripple effects run even deeper into the global economy. Prochemical production relies heavily on oil and gas feed stocks. Semiconductor supply chains depend on predictable shipping routes and specialized industrial materials. Gulf sovereign wealth funds manage trillions of dollars in assets worldwide. So any instability that forces them to move their capital can echo across financial markets. Taken together, these examples reveal just how many critical systems underpin the global economy. A prolonged conflict with Iran will shape prices, supply chains, and growth across the planet. And as those disruptions mount, the White House will gradually yield to investors and markets. Politics is the third and final pressure point. It's less visible than weapons or markets, but just as powerful. While military campaigns can stretch for years, elections arrive on schedule. And that mismatch eventually creates pressure. At the start of a conflict, political leaders usually enjoy broad public support. Governments have room to act and military operations move forward with relatively little domestic resistance. But that unity rarely lasts forever. As hostilities drag on, questions begin to surface. What are the objectives? How long will this continue? What are the costs? Those questions grow louder once the war begins to affect everyday life, whether through rising fuel costs, higher inflation, or the steady drip of casualties. In the United States, the next political clock is always ticking. Every 2 years, Americans elect a new Congress. The next one is scheduled for November 2026. In that election, all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and roughly onethird of the seats in the Senate will be on the ballot. These midterm elections often become a referendum on the sitting president's policies, especially during periods of economic stress or military conflict. A war that drags on too long, can quickly turn into a political liability, even if the fighting itself remains far away. Lawmakers, particularly those from swing districts and swing states, are usually the first to distance themselves from unpopular policies. Not necessarily because the war has been lost, but because the domestic political environment can no longer sustain it. For a president, that creates a dilemma. Armies can fight for as long as their supplies last. Economies can absorb shocks for a time. But political legitimacy must be renewed at the ballot box. So if the war with Iran drags on long enough to collide with the midterm election, the pressure will not only come from the battlefield or the markets, it will also come from Capitol Hill. When viewed together, munitions, markets, and midterms will determine the outcome of this conflict. Each of these pressure points can shape political decisions. Iran understands this dynamic and leans into it. The attacks on tankers and data centers are meant to stretch missile supply chains, unsettle global markets, and wait for political pressure in Washington to build. And as these pressure points converge at the same time, they will begin to narrow Trump's room for maneuver. Before long, total victory is spun into acceptable outcome. That would be the tradeoff. glossary.title: If You Don't Understand the Petrodollar, You Don't Understand Money
glossary.llm_summary: The petrodollar system: in 1974, Kissinger made a deal with Saudi Arabia — sell oil only in USD, US provides military protection. Every oil-importing country (effectively everyone) must hold dollars to buy energy, creating permanent structural demand for USD regardless of US economic performance. Petrodollar recycling: Saudi/Gulf sovereign wealth reinvests oil revenues into US debt, stocks, and real estate — money flows out to buy oil then straight back in as investment. This gives the US three permanent advantages: stronger dollar than fundamentals justify, lower bond yields (everyone must hold US treasuries), and the ability to economically destroy countries via sanctions (Russia 2022 example). The system is now cracking: China/Russia/India/Saudi Arabia are trading oil in non-dollar currencies. Dollar's share of global reserves has fallen from 70% to 58%. Felix argues the petrodollar is in its 'newspaper moment' — won't collapse suddenly but will erode trade-by-trade. For ASX: dollar decline benefits AUD (commodity currency), commodity exporters, and energy transition stocks.

glossary.transcript_text: Gamblers's ruin. The fundamental idea behind gamblers's ruin is that in any game of chance where the gambler has finite capital and a non-positive expected value. It is statistically certain that the gambler will eventually hit a string of bad luck and go bankrupt. And it's not because the gamblers are stupid or because they're reckless, but it's because you have a nonpositive expected value and time is working against you. Let's say you're playing roulette and you only bet black. There are 38 pockets on a roulette board and 18 are black. This means you have a little over a 47% chance to win. So, you play a few rounds and you get on a winning streak. But that's where the gambler's ruin concept starts to set in because every single spin of the roulette wheel has a negative expected value because a 47% win rate means you have a 53% chance to lose. And because of this, you will eventually hit a bad streak. And that's why the casinos don't need to cheat you. They just wait and let time do the work. Because the longer you play, the more certain your losses become.

glossary.title: Iran has a new Supreme Leader. Does it even matter?
glossary.llm_summary: Khamenei was killed in US-Israeli strikes and Iran's Assembly of Experts selected his son Moshtaba as Supreme Leader within days — not through procedure but through IRGC pressure (described as a coup dressed as succession). Moshtaba is a former IRGC officer, personally lost family members in the strikes, and is a strong advocate of the axis of resistance (Lebanon, Yemen, Iraq proxies). He rose after Ibrahim Raisi died in a helicopter crash in 2024. A three-person wartime council — moderate president Peshkan, hardline judiciary head, and senior cleric — is holding power in parallel. Senior IRGC commanders are being systematically killed by Israeli strikes, creating internal power flux. Iran doesn't need a Supreme Leader to launch missiles, but succession stability matters for post-war Iran. The IRGC remains the real kingmaker. Leadership uncertainty prolongs the conflict and sustains the geopolitical risk premium on energy.
glossary.transcript_text: Ayatah Ali Kame the man who had personified the Islamic Republic for nearly four decades is dead. Within days Iran's assembly of experts had chosen his son Moshtaba as the country's new supreme leader. The speed of that decision says less about the strength of Iran's institutions than it does about who truly runs the country. You see, in the Islamic Republic, formal authority and real power are not the same thing. While clerics hold titles and names, they do not always decide how leadership passes from one to the next. Behind the religious establishment stands the revolutionary guards, Iran's most powerful institution, and in moments like this, the ultimate kingmaker. So for all intents and purposes, the IRGC has essentially staged a coup and called it succession. But while Moshtaba's election ends the immediate succession crisis, it does not bring stability. As the new supreme leader, he inherits a country at war and there is no telling how long he can hold power as bombs continue to fall across its cities. And so the real question was never about who replaces KA, but whether Iran's political system can survive the war long enough for any succession to matter. As much as the Supreme Leader had appropriated the levers of power, it was still a system. So, even though the Supreme Leader had the final say on all matters in the country, he only arrived at decisions after a lengthy consultative process. Whatever one may think of the Islamic Republic as a state, it has formal institutions, codified procedures, contingency plans, and mechanisms for continuity of government, even if those institutions are sometimes shaky. In the first two days of this war, numerous top officials had already been taken out, including the commander of the revolutionary guards, the defense minister, the chief of staff of the armed forces, and the secretary of the defense council. Iran has regulations and procedures, but its political system is also complex, intricate, and somewhat confusing. The top factions compete fiercely, particularly over succession and the path the Islamic Republic should take in both domestic and foreign affairs. The revolutionary guards are without doubt the dominant force, the kingmakers, if you will. glossary.title: Is Oil the Next Commodity to Rip? (Josh Young)
glossary.llm_summary:
Josh Young (Bison Interests, Houston) makes the case that oil is the next commodity cycle to run, directly paralleling the experience of mining investors who have watched copper, gold, and lithium lead first.

Supply side: US shale has been kept alive by technology (laterals extended from 1 mile to 4 miles, massively reducing per-well capex), but this is now rolling over in 2026 — drilling must grow just to stay flat due to 5-8% global decline rates. Canada is effectively landlocked (no new pipelines approved, government redirecting royalty revenue from Alberta). Brazil is near capacity at 4M bbl/day. Ghana cannot scale from 1M to 3M. New supply is genuinely unclear.

Demand side: Josh's base case is >1% demand growth per year, which no major agency (IEA, OPEC, banks) is forecasting through 2050 — despite actual recent data showing 2.1-2.4M bbl/day growth in a single year. He argues China is likely understating oil consumption and inflating storage data to buy crude $10/barrel cheaper (a strategy consistent with how Chinese counterparties behave in physical oil trades, per the traders he has spoken to).

Data quality: The oil market data is described as "abysmal" — the EIA published a figure of 24M bbl/day US liquids production which Josh calls clearly wrong (double-counting refinery output). Every major provider is "wrong all the time."

The single most important variable: "If the US bombs Iran" — identified in the opening as the factor that would matter more for oil markets than anything else over a 12-month horizon. This was recorded before the Iran war started, making it prescient.

Valuation: Oil majors (Exxon etc.) are expensive, earnings declining as stocks rise. Best value is oil field services — drilling rigs, offshore drillers, completion companies — trading at large discounts to replacement cost and cheap cash flow multiples. Josh draws explicit parallel to Australian mining services stocks. Direct ASX read-through: energy producers (WDS, STO) and oil field services exposed. Oil price above $100 is an inflation shock for RBA and ASX rate-sensitive sectors.

These include the 2017 to 2018 economic protests, the 2019 to 2020 fuel protests, the 2021 to 2022 water protests, the 2022 to 2023 women's rights protests, and most recently the current protests. In short, Iran has been down this road before. However, the current protests are different and this chart tells the story you need to know. The Iranian realale has plummeted against the US dollar since the Israel Iran war, losing about 40% of its value in less than 7 months. In late December, things finally snapped. Shopkeepers in Thyron's Grand Bazaar and other commercial districts took to the streets. Within days, the demonstrations spread to other commercial centers nationwide and expanded to include activists, students, truck drivers, and others. The economic frustrations of Iranians had been simmering for years. In fact, President Peshkan was elected in 2024 precisely because he promised to negotiate a new nuclear deal with the United States to ease sanctions. However, the talks failed. Both sides adopted maximalist positions, offering little to no compromise. Then, in June 2025, the Israeli and American strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities compounded the diplomatic deadlock. Policymakers in Thran looked inward with little hope of sanctions relief and lacking the capacity to address its economic shortcomings. Iranian political factions began pointing fingers at one another. Among other measures, the minister of economic affairs was dismissed and the central bank governor was later replaced. But this reshuffleling has had no impact on the livelihoods of ordinary citizens and merely demonstrates how the political elite in Thran moves lawmakers in and out of government just to appease a frustrated population since they have no real way to improve the economy. Iran's economic policy is essentially a menu with nothing worth ordering. Regardless of how many people are in the streets, the government in Thran has no intention of giving up. They will not go down without a fight, and they're willing to risk civil war if it comes to it. That's because Iran's socopolitical state is extremely complicated and will remain so for the foreseeable future. Whether one likes the clergy or not, Thran has a stable support base. In the last presidential election, over 13 million people voted for the ultraconservative candidate. This support base underpins the government, the IRGC, and other paramilitary groups. It's essentially what keeps the country running despite all its complications and shortcomings. So even if protesters prevail, the government machinery will not disappear overnight. It's also worth noting that Iran's government is not a monolith. Behind the scenes, there are disagreements over policym and what steps the state should take. This is important to understand because contrary to the belief that the protests will cause the government to collapse, it's more likely that the protests will drive political change from within by reinforcing certain political elements while disarming others. Whether that means a dramatic change in policy led by liberal officials such as President Peshkan, Ali Larijani or former President Roani remains to be seen. But it could just as easily mean an extreme change in the opposite direction with IRGC officials taking direct responsibility for the country. At the same time, it should be noted that within Iran, there is no organized political opposition to the government. They've been co-opted by the state. Meanwhile, outside the country, the political opposition is highly conflicted and polarized. Some of the groups include communists, Republicans, and monarchists like Palavi. Apart from their opposition to the Islamic Republic, they share little in common. In this round of protests, the monarchists have had the upper hand. They've successfully spread disinformation at scale, particularly online, but their on the ground influence is limited. Another point to remember is that many Iranians who oppose the government also fear that a collapse would lead to an unpredictable power vacuum and possibly the disintegration of Iran into many smaller countries based on ethnic fault lines. Thus, even Iranians who oppose the government acknowledge that the current system provides some degree of national unity even if that unity is coerced. Perhaps the soft underbelly of the government machinery, specifically within its security apparatus, is the army. For context, Iran has a regular military like every other nation, but it also has the IRGC, also known as the Revolutionary Guards. This faction has the numbers and weapons and frankly overshadows the regular army. It's doubtful that Iran will see defections within the Revolutionary Guard, primarily because they are financially and politically entrenched in the current political system. For the protests to truly endanger the government, this massive apparatus would first need to fall apart, and the regular army could be a weak spot to watch. Its members are less devout and less committed to the Supreme Leader, which is also why they've always come second to the IRGC in equipment and armaments. So, if there are any security defectors, they will come from the regular army. The bottom line is that Thran is facing massive demonstrations, one of the most serious since the 1979 revolution. However, don't expect a rerun of Syria, where Assad was ousted in a matter of days. The Iranian state still has broad pockets of support across the country and can weather the current unrest for weeks to come before crackdowns suppress it. That window, however, also leaves Iran's leadership in the crosshairs of American or Israeli power, visible or otherwise. I've been your host, Shivan, from Caspian Report. glossary.title: What's next for Venezuela?
glossary.llm_summary: US raided Venezuela and captured Maduro; transition is fragile. Power rests not in Maduro but in a coalition of patronage, oil revenues, and hard power. Defence Minister Padrino controls the armed forces; Interior Minister Cabello commands the paramilitary collectivos — both under US sanctions with no sign of surrendering. Trump wants Vice President Rodriguez as interim leader conditional on expelling Colombian guerrillas, downgrading Russia/China ties, and dismantling illicit flows — demands that threaten the military factions who profit from them. Venezuela produces ~1 million barrels/day, far below its 3.5 million late-1990s peak. The 300 billion barrel reserve estimate is potentially fabricated (Hugo Chavez coerced PDVSA to triple estimates in the late 2000s for political leverage). Three outcomes: managed transition (best case, unlikely), continuity without Maduro (most likely), or fragmentation into violent elite power struggle. Minimal direct ASX impact.
glossary.transcript_text: America's raid on Venezuela has paid off. Or so it seems. Trump is now signaling that he can force Caracus back into line, open the door to new energy deals on US terms, and curb the influence of rival powers in the hemisphere. And while the optics suggest closure, reality points to the start of a far more difficult and dangerous phase. For two decades, Venezuela has been the single largest driver of regional instability, fueling mass migration, crossber crime, and economic distress across the continent. And so from Washington's perspective, stabilizing Venezuela is not just about oil or geopolitics. It is about tackling the sources of those problems before they reach the US border. But history warns against easy victories. When the United States toppled Saddam in 2003, the mission quickly collapsed into insurgency, fractured authority, and years of costly involvement. Venezuela now sits at a similar inflection point. Removing Maduro may clear the path for a genuine political transition, but it could just as easily pull America into open-ended commitments. Sometimes even superpowers trip over their own shadow. Maduro is unlikely to see daylight anytime soon, but his removal does not mean the ruin of Venezuela's government or the end of Chavismo as an ideology. Power in Karakas has never rested in a single institution. It functions as a coalition stitched together by patronage, access to oil revenues, and control over hard power. With the arbitrator of that system gone, the coalition is now at risk of splintering. The decisive variable is the military. Some commanders will move quickly to bargain with whatever authority emerges. Others will hold out, betting that uncertainty works in their favor. Civilian power brokers such as governors, party officials, and business tycoons will move the same way, hedging rather than committing. Trump, however, has other plans. He prefers Vice President Deli Rodriguez as interim leader on the condition that she delivers on US demands. If she fails, the White House has threatened to use its naval task force in the Caribbean to cut off oil exports. Venezuela's economic lifeline. But it's not that black and white. Rodriguez sits in a trap of her own. If she complies fully with Trump's demands, she risks being toppled as a traitor by hardliners within the ruling party. At the same time, if she goes against Trump, she could face a fate worse than that of Maduro. Some of Trump's demands are transactional. Giving America a bigger role in Venezuela's oil sector is something Rodriguez can realistically deliver. As vice president, she helped negotiate many of the existing contracts. But the other demands such as downgrading ties with Russia and China, expelling Colombian Marxist guerrillas, and dismantling the illicit flows that go through the country are more complicated. Meeting those conditions would directly threaten the military factions that profit from them and set Rodriguez against some very powerful associates. Long-erving defense minister Vladimir Padrino and Interior Minister Diostad Cabo control most of Venezuela's hard power. Padrino runs the armed forces while Cababelloo commands the collectivos which is a collection of paramilitary forces used to intimidate rivals and snuff out descent. Both figures remain under US sanctions and neither has shown any indication of surrendering power. In the foreseeable future, Venezuela will likely see an intensified violent struggle among these power brokers rather than consolidation. Meanwhile, Venezuela's democratic opposition is under pressure to act and may take matters into its own hands. Many Venezuelans are disheartened that Maduro's ousting has led to a government that looks identical to the previous one they despised minus the leader. These distraught citizens could take to the streets and try to topple Chavismo altogether. Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has urged that her ally Edmundo Gonzalez be recognized as the legitimate successor to the disputed 20124 election. Washington and several foreign governments had endorsed that position at the time. However, Machado has so far stopped short of calling mass mobilization inside the country, telling them only to be ready for what comes next. She has vowed to return to Venezuela, which could galvanize mass protests [music] against the government. Keeping a lid on all these moving elements, is not easy. A peaceful transition is still possible, but only if the process offers calibrated pressure, political amnesty, and a road map towards reintegration rather than blanket punishment. Without such measures, spoilers will emerge. Not only ideological hardliners, but rational actors acting in self-preservation. [music] Maduro's exit does not dismantle the ecosystem he left behind. Crowds are restless. Political officials are scrambling for leverage. Militias and criminal networks are watching for openings. and [music] insurgent groups on the margins are set to take advantage of any chaos that emerges in the coming days and weeks. The balance sheet rather than the battlefield could prove to be the key. Venezuela has lost more than 3/4 of its GDP over the past decade. Oil production has collapsed. Public services barely function. Inflation is skyhigh and malnutrition is widespread. No other disaster in South America compares in scale. Seen in this way, control over oil revenues is not just a technical issue. It is the central determinant of whether any future government can govern at all. If those energy revenues are captured, frozen, or used as leverage by the United States, national sovereignty becomes hollow, regardless of democratic elections. [music] So, Venezuela's future hinges on who controls its hydrocarbon wealth and how it's put to work. Today, the country produces roughly 1 million barrels per day, far lower than the 3.5 million it pumped in the late 1990s. Official reserves are often cited at more than 300 billion barrels, but there's a problem. It may be entirely made up. For context, Venezuela does hold massive oil reserves, but the 300 billion estimate comes from JP Morgan, which cites an OPEC report. The caveat is that OPEC relies solely on the numbers provided by its members, not independent audits. Venezuela's state-owned oil and gas company, the PDVSA, tripled its reserve estimate [music] in the late 2000s without the appropriate exploration. At the time, Hugo Chavez needed a win to bolster his international leverage and thus coerced the PDVSA into inflating the numbers. Hence, the 300 billion may be entirely made up. Even if the upper estimate proves accurate, the commercial reality is harsh. Much of Venezuela's output is heavy crude. It's high in sulfur and metallic impurities. US refiners can still convert it into jet fuel, but doing so is costly, which crushes margins and drives a steep discount relative to Texas light, sweet crude. A realistic conversation about Venezuela's hydrocarbon resources is essential. If the country has a true cushion of 300 billion barrels, reconstruction has room for mistakes. But if the workable number is closer to 100 billion and concentrated in technically complex fields, the margin for error slims down. In that stage, corruption, patronage, and mismanagement would not just slow Venezuela's recovery, they could kill it. Three outcomes now sit in front of Venezuela. The first is a managed transition. Elections could be held, but whether a single opposition figure emerges as a viable leader remains uncertain. Machado has political drive, but that means little considering the environment in which she operates. Venezuela's political system is fractured. Its institutions are weak, and powerful security actors hold veto power. Years of exile and repression have [music] thinned the opposition's depth. Power could instead settle around an interim or technocratic council that is acceptable to the armed forces and parts of the former government. This option offers the best chance of stabilization, but only if paired with economic relief and credible guarantees for those relinquishing power. This would of course be the preferred outcome for Venezuelans, but the final say seldom belongs to the public. The second outcome is the continuity of the current system, only [music] without Maduro. The government's coercive and illicit machinery survives the leadership change. Armed groups continue to operate. Political change becomes cosmetic and all the while socioeconomic instability persists. Authority could be formally handed to a civilian caretaker such as Rodriguez who would then provide bureaucratic continuity abroad while preserving the power structures at home. For what it's worth, this is the most likely outcome in the immediate future. The third outcome is escalation. Elite power struggles turn violent. Armed actors multiply and violence spreads from the barracks to the streets. Military officers, collectivos, and criminal networks carve out new territories and revenue streams while security services cease to obey the chain of command. The United States, having claimed ownership of the Maduro raid, is pulled back in. This time, not by choice, but by momentum. What begins as crisis management turns into force protection, convoy security, and political mediation. The mission blurs into an open-ended commitment with rising costs, shrinking leverage, and no clean exit. Which of these three outcomes comes true will depend less on Maduro's removal than on the US strategy that follows. Venezuela is now a testing ground for American power and judgment. There will be a strong temptation to declare victory and walk away, but that would be reckless. Trying to engineer every outcome would be worse. Before we end, there's one more thing worth paying attention to, and it has to do with today's sponsor, Vanguard Mining, traded under the ticker UUFF on Schwab, Fidelity, Interactive Brokers, [music] and Erade. The raid on Venezuela shows what happens when strategic resources fall under sanctions or foreign leverage. And oil is just the start. Today, the real pressure points are critical minerals, items that most people never really think about, but they form the building blocks of energy systems, defense industries, and industrial power. And in several of them, China holds decisive leverage over the West. Vanguard Mining has repositioned itself around this shift. Its portfolio is built around five strategic metals. Gold, copper, lithium, uranium, and malibdinum. Just as important, its projects are located in jurisdictions aligned with western supply chains including Canada, Argentina, and Paraguay. Vanguard holds a gold, copper, and malibdinum [music] project in British Columbia. The latter is a quiet but essential metal that is now subject to Chinese export restrictions. Vanguard also controls more than 90,000 [music] hectares in Paraguay's Parana Basin right next to a major uranium project. The company has also regained full ownership of the Positos one lithium project in Argentina just as lithium prices rebound. This race for mineral resources is all about resilience. Companies positioned across multiple metals and friendly jurisdictions are central to how the next [music] phase of global competition plays out and Vanguard is in prime position to be part of that. Check out their ticker on the screen and learn more by clicking the link in the description. Just make sure to do your own due diligence. I've been your host Shivan from Caspian Report. If you approve of what we do, please leave a comment, hit the like button, and mayhaps share the video. In any case, thank you for your time and s [music] >> [music]

glossary.title: Why global debt keeps growing ($345 trillion and counting)
glossary.llm_summary: Nixon severed the dollar-gold link on August 15, 1971 — from that point governments gained the ability to create money at will and global debt took on a life of its own, growing from billions to $345 trillion today (3x global GDP). The US alone owes $38 trillion, 70% to its own citizens through the bank-pension-insurance loop (US commercial banks hold $4.6 trillion in Treasury bonds). The remaining 30% is foreign-held. The system is self-reinforcing: to repay old debt, governments borrow more; economies require constant money circulation to function; stopping overnight would collapse public spending and trigger recession (as nearly happened in COVID). The risk is perception-driven — when confidence breaks, borrowing costs spike, forcing governments to choose between spending cuts, tax hikes, or money printing (inflation). Zimbabwe 2008 is the extreme case. For ASX: structural global debt and money printing sustain inflation expectations, support commodity prices long-term, and pressure central banks including the RBA.
glossary.transcript_text: It's August 15th, 1971. President Richard Nixon appears on live television and announces that the United States will no longer convert dollars into gold. >> I have directed Secretary Connley to suspend temporarily the convertability of the dollar into gold or other reserve assets. >> It seems like a minor technicality, but what follows is monumental. Money once anchored to something physical becomes pure fiat currency backed by nothing more than government decree. Immediately thereafter things begin to change. Global debt takes a life of its own and over the next few decades it balloons from billions to trillions. Today it stands at $345 trillion give or take. That's three times the size of the entire global economy. America alone accounts for 38 trillion of that. But there's something strange about all this. You see, the US owes China roughly $770 billion. Yet, China itself is drowning in $18 trillion worth of debt. Much of it sits with Chinese banks, the same banks that also own American debt. American banks, in turn, are holding debt from China, Europe, and just about everyone else. But here's the paradox. If everyone owes money to everyone else, then who is all that money actually going to? The answer isn't what you think. Follow the money far enough, and the trail circles back to where it started. The world essentially owes money to itself, and it works so long as no one checks the math. Today's video is sponsored by Sift. Every day, we're flooded with information. There are too many headlines, too little context, and half the story is happening in languages most of us don't even see or understand. Sift takes a completely different approach. Instead of chasing headlines, you start with a topic you actually care about. SIFT then scans trusted local and global sources across countries and languages and translates and summarizes the key developments into one clear readable feed. So you're not just seeing how a story is framed, you're seeing what's actually happening, often before it reaches mainstream coverage. It's less about comparing headlines and more about following how a topic actually evolves around the world. It's loved by thousands of people and is even the number one ranking news app in several countries. Sift builds a personalized feed around whatever you want to follow. And because it pulls from local sources worldwide, you get broader coverage, real context, and clarity you won't get from just one country's media without bouncing between the apps. It also stays on top of updates with realtime coverage and notifications. And if you want the full context, [music] you can always click through and go deeper. So if you want to actually understand what's happening in the world, not just scroll past it, search SIFT and download the app for free on the App Store or Google Play. Debt is as old as civilization itself. Long before banks or paper money, debt was simply a promise. A neighbor lends you a bag of grain in spring and come harvest you pay them back maybe with a little extra as thanks. This is how societies operated for thousands of years. However, as trade expanded beyond local communities, these arrangements grew more complex. During the Renaissance, Italian banking houses created credit instruments, ways to transfer debt rather than just hold it personally. This allowed merchants to do business across continents without carrying chests of gold. The real breakthrough, however, came in 1694 when Britain faced a funding crisis under King William III. The Royal Navy desperately needed 1.2 million to finance the war with France, but the government's credit was poor and [music] direct borrowing proved impossible. So the royal court came up with an ingenious solution. Create a corporation called the Bank of England and allow investors to become shareholders. The bank would then lend the money to the government and charge 8% interest. In return, it received government bonds which could be resold to the public or to anyone willing to buy them. Suddenly, for the first time, ordinary citizens could effectively lend money to the state through a reliable agent. It was a simple scheme, but it changed everything. States could now raise massive sums without hiking taxes or draining their treasuries. The system quickly spread across Europe and became the bedrock of early capitalism. Then, during the industrial revolution, the system went into overdrive. Factories, railroads, and infrastructure required unprecedented amounts of capital, far more than any single wealthy individual could muster. The banks that had been set up pulled saving deposits and lent them to industrialists. By doing so, borrowing became not just useful, but structurally necessary for economic growth. By the 20th century, World War I and World War II pushed countries to borrow at scales never before seen, not just to fight, but to rebuild afterward. In 1944, the Breton Woods agreement made the US dollar the centerpiece of the global financial system with currencies tied to the dollar and the dollar tied to gold. But gold was limited and economies had to grow. So, as US spending accelerated during the Vietnam War and the Great Society programs, there wasn't enough gold to back the flood of dollars circulating globally, forcing Nixon to sever the link in 1971. The consequences were profound. From that point forward, governments gained the ability to create money at will. And with the old restraints gone, a new system emerged where debt could expand as long as lenders remained confident in government decrees. Steadily throughout the 1980s, nations discovered that borrowing wasn't just useful in wartime. It could fuel peacetime growth, too. And so, governments borrowed to build schools, repair roads, and pull economies out of recession. Debt stopped being a last resort and became standard operating procedure. Today, debt is how things get built, how recessions are managed, and how political promises are kept. Debt is no longer an anomaly in the system. It has become the system itself. The United States offers the clearest example of how this self-reinforcing system actually works. With $ 38 trillion in debt, no other country comes even close. Yet, roughly 70% of that debt is owed to Americans themselves. The US in essence borrows from its own citizens. You see, when someone deposits money in a bank, it doesn't just sit in a vault. Banks put that money to work trying to grow it so they can pass some interest back to depositors. They do this by lending, investing, and buying bonds. Right now, US commercial banks hold about $4.6 trillion in Treasury bonds and other government securities, which is more than the GDP of Japan or India. Bonds are particularly popular because they're one of the safest ways to earn interest. [music] And unlike stocks that swing wildly every day, a 10-year US government bond today pays a steady annual interest rate, offering reliable returns with little risk. But banks aren't alone in this. Pension funds, insurance companies, and investment firms all do the same. So essentially, private savings have become an indirect form of government borrowing. And although it sounds odd that the US borrows from itself, think of it as money moving from parts of the country where it's sitting idle to parts where it's needed. When the government pays interest on its debt, the money flows back to lenders, giving them more cash to buy more bonds and earn more interest. It's a closed loop where money cycles endlessly from lender to borrower and back again. The same loop exists between countries. About 30% of US debt is held overseas. Foreign governments and banks buy US bonds the same way American institutions do. Money flows into the US when it borrows, flows back out when it pays interest, and the cycle repeats. And it's not just America that does this. Every country borrows, and every country lends. Japanese savings are turned into loans for the Saudis. Saudi savings become loans for Brazilians. Brazilian capital flows back into US bonds. This interconnected web creates an uneasy reality. To repay debts, governments must keep borrowing more and more. That may sound reckless, and in many ways it is, but it's also the foundation of how the global economy now works. >> [music] >> Everything from economic growth to political stability depends on this endless cycle continuing. Since debt fuels growth, governments have no choice but to borrow and spend and get money circulating in the economy. By doing so, businesses earn more. Workers get paid and as a result, they spend more. It becomes a feedback loop that keeps the economy expanding. >> [music] >> In China, about a fifth of government spending is financed by borrowing. In the US, it's one in every $4. If governments stopped borrowing overnight, public spending would fall immediately. Money would stop flowing into the economy, businesses would earn less, layoffs would increase, and [music] consumer spending would grind to a stop. That's precisely what happened when COVID hit in 2020. As people stopped spending and the economy shut down, governments stepped in and covered expenses people were unwilling to pay. In America, the government borrowed $3.1 trillion in a single year, which was about 12% of the economy at the time. China, Europe, and every other major economy did the same. It wasn't a choice [music] really. It was necessity. However, borrowed money must eventually be returned. If a government already spends everything it collects to keep the economy going, then it must take out new loans to repay the old ones. So, the debt never truly leaves the system. It just adds up. Wealthier countries such as Germany and Switzerland can afford to cycle through this system. Their bonds are considered safe, so they keep borrowing at low interest rates. But for developing nations, it's different. Higher borrowing costs make each rollover more expensive. Over time, debt starts to feed on itself. Countries like Kenya and Pakistan, for instance, are stuck in debt traps and forced to keep borrowing just to meet interest payments on past loans. So, the same debt that strengthens some economies can end up holding others back. >> [music] >> Debt-driven economies carry inherent dangers. No matter how smooth the cycle seems, risks are building beneath the surface. As governments continue borrowing, debt grows and so do interest payments. Over time, a bigger slice of the budget goes toward paying off old loans rather than funding schools, hospitals, or infrastructure. A debt to GDP ratio of about 100% is now considered normal. And frankly, debt is not a problem so long as borrowing is cheap and lenders are confident. But when political risks change and investors stop wanting to lend, borrowing costs shoot up. So perception is the real driver of the economy. One way governments keep a lid on things is by printing more money. Banks call it quantitative easing. The problem, however, is that when more money enters circulation, the value of each unit declines. The result is inflation and higher everyday costs. In extreme cases, it spirals out of control. In Zimbabwe in 2008, the government printed so much money to cover debts that prices doubled every single day. A loaf of bread that cost 10 million Zimbabwe dollars in March suddenly cost hundreds of millions by midyear and billions by November. The government eventually printed $100 trillion notes to cope with the situation, but that only made it worse. The currency became worthless and ordinary people saw their life savings vanish overnight. While most countries don't face such extremes, even moderate inflation can hurt. The risks are even bigger for developing countries which often borrow in foreign currencies such as US dollars. Meaning when their own currency weakens, debt repayments suddenly become more expensive in local terms. And as that burden grows, lenders start doubting the country's ability to repay. That's pretty much what happened in Turkey. Once the mood shifts and doubt sets in, investors tend to demand higher interest rates to compensate for the risks. And when borrowing hits a wall, governments are forced into ugly tradeoffs. They can either cut spending, raise taxes, or expand the money supply. Each of these options comes with severe consequences. All in all, the global economy is wired for constant momentum. Debt isn't a flaw. It's what keeps nations running, borrowing, lending, spending, and starting over. This perpetual motion, however, can't keep going forever. Eventually, there will be a reckoning, an economic depression. Centuries ago, physics proved that perpetual motion is impossible. Economics is yet to come around. Before we wrap up, a quick shout out to Search Party. They produce sharp, well-ressearched videos on global affairs. And if you enjoy this channel, you'll get value there, too. The link is below. I've been your host, Shivan from Caspian Report. If you approve of what we do, please leave a comment, hit the like button, and mayhaps share the video. In any case, thank you for your time and So [music] [music]
